finding.claim: DELETE /reports/:id deletes the report even when the caller lacks delete grant, because authorize() is not awaited, so its 403 throw becomes an unhandled rejection and the delete proceeds. Any caller with a session object (including one with no user) can delete any report.
finding.source: req.params.id (URL path) and req.user from req.session.user (server.js:5)

trace.note: req.user = req.session.user; no session middleware in this file, so the session is assumed to exist
DELETE /reports/:id handler, no route-level auth guard
report loaded by attacker-supplied id, no owner or tenant check
authorize(req.user, 'delete', report) called without await; returns a Promise that is discarded
authorize is async, so the throw at line 14 becomes a rejected Promise
db.grants(user.id, ...) throws TypeError if req.user is undefined, also producing an unhandled rejection
delete executes regardless of the authorization result

finding.guards_checked: Grant check at lines 9-16 is correct but only effective if awaited; it is not awaited at line 20. No try/catch, no .catch, no route or global auth middleware, no authorization in the database layer visible from this file. Node 15+ default unhandled-rejection behavior can crash the process on a denied delete (availability impact).

verdict.guard_found: None effective. The only grant check is authorize() at server.js:9-16, but its result is never tested: server.js:20 calls it without await, so the rejection from the throw at server.js:14 is not observed and server.js:21 runs. No try/catch, no route-level or global auth guard beyond the session-copy middleware at server.js:4-7, which does not check grants. The only other authorization call (server.js:27, PUT) is awaited, which confirms the DELETE omission is a bug and not a design choice.
verdict.reason: server.js:20 calls authorize(req.user, "delete", report) without await, so its 403 at server.js:14 becomes a discarded rejected promise and server.js:21 deletes the report regardless of the grant check. Any authenticated user who can reach the route (the attacker only needs a session, not delete rights) can delete any report by id; the candidate's "no user" variant also holds since db.grants(user.id) at server.js:10 throws and the delete still proceeds. Caveat: the session middleware that populates req.session lives outside this file, so the reachable population is assumed rather than shown, and db is not defined in server.js.

finding.claim: PUT /reports/:id passes the raw request body to the database update, so a user with only the write grant can set arbitrary report fields (potentially owner, tenant, or other protected columns). Impact depends on the reports schema, which is not in the repo, so confidence is plausible rather than confirmed.
finding.source: req.body parsed by express.json() (server.js:3), reached via PUT /reports/:id

trace.note: app.use(express.json()) parses the request body into req.body without filtering
await authorize(req.user, 'write', report) passes for a user with write grant
entire req.body passed to db.reports.update with no field allowlist

finding.guards_checked: The write grant check at line 27 is correct and awaited. No field allowlist, schema validation, or ownership-field protection exists in server.js. The db module is absent from the repo, so the database layer's own filtering could not be verified.

verdict.guard_found: authorize() at server.js:9-16 throws a 403 when the 'write' grant is missing, and it is awaited at server.js:27, so it blocks users without write on the report. No field allowlist, schema validation, or protection of owner/tenant fields exists in server.js, and the db module is not in the repo.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches server.js (3, 25-28), and the write check at server.js:27 correctly throws for users without the grant, so the only open question is whether a write-grant holder can reach protected columns; server.js:28 passes the whole req.body to db.reports.update, but the reports schema and the db layer's own filtering are not in the repo, so impact cannot be confirmed.

finding.claim: A denied PUT (no write grant, or req.user undefined) throws inside an async handler; on Express 4 the rejection is not forwarded to error middleware, so the request hangs and, on Node 15+, the unhandled rejection can crash the process. This is an availability issue, not an authorization bypass.
finding.sink: Unhandled Promise rejection from await authorize() at server.js:27, crashing the process or leaving the request open

trace.note: async PUT handler registered directly on Express app
await authorize throws 403 for caller without write grant
res.json never reached; no try/catch or error forwarding

finding.guards_checked: Authorization itself is enforced correctly (the rejection prevents the update). No try/catch or async error wrapper exists. Express version is not pinned in the repo, so whether the rejection is forwarded depends on the runtime (Express 5 forwards it).

verdict.guard_found: none. authorize() (server.js:9-16) throws on failure, and the PUT handler awaits it at line 27, so the 403 does reject the handler promise. No try/catch, error wrapper, or Express error handler exists in server.js.
verdict.reason: The trace is off by one: res.json is at server.js:29, while line 30 is only the closing `});`. Whether the rejection at server.js:27 crashes or hangs the process depends on the Express version, and no package.json exists in the directory to pin it. On Express 4 the claim holds, but on Express 5 (the current default for a fresh install) the rejection is forwarded to error middleware, so the verdict cannot be decided from the code provided.
